name: Loan Management Systems
description: Loan management systems support the administration of credit from approval through repayment and the handling of troubled exposures. Understanding their role in Iran requires separating software capabilities from lending policy, portfolio quality, and verified institutional practice.

seo.title: Loan Management Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How credit administration, monitoring, and problem-loan management fit together, with evidence limits for Iranian banking implementations.

content.heading: Following credit beyond approval
content.content:
A lending decision begins an ongoing administrative relationship. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, an international banking standard setter, organizes credit-risk management around policy, credit granting, administration and monitoring, and controls. Its revised principles provide a useful framework for understanding loan-management software; they do not establish which functions Iranian banks have implemented. [s1]

Credit administration includes maintaining files, obtaining updated financial information, tracking contractual requirements and collateral, and supplying accurate management information. Software can organize these tasks, but assessment of a borrower's capacity to repay remains a substantive credit responsibility. An electronic record is useful only when it preserves the information needed to understand the exposure. [s2]

content.heading: Why the Iranian context matters
content.content:
The International Monetary Fund's staff report for Iran's 2018 consultation called for stronger credit-risk management and governance in state-owned banks, alongside measures addressing directed lending and government obligations to banks. This was a historical diagnosis and reform recommendation, not an assessment of current software or proof that the proposed reforms were completed. [s3]

The distinction matters when evaluating technology claims. A system may record an approval consistently while the underlying lending decision remains weak. Conversely, a sound credit policy needs reliable administration to reveal whether contractual obligations are being met. The international framework therefore treats controls and monitoring as integral parts of lending rather than optional additions after disbursement. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Monitoring, exceptions, and review
content.content:
Basel guidance emphasizes independent review, attention to limit breaches, and early remedial action when credit quality deteriorates. For readers assessing a loan-management system, the practical questions concern evidence: can reviewers trace changes, identify exceptions, and distinguish an approved contractual amendment from an unresolved payment problem? These are evaluation questions derived from the guidance, not verified descriptions of any Iranian bank. [s2]

Consistent data definitions also matter. Basel's risk-data principles call for reliable aggregation and reconciliation with source information, including accounting data where appropriate. A portfolio report should therefore be explainable from its underlying records. [s4]

This page establishes the functional framework. A fuller Iranian account requires current contract documentation, supervisory instructions, and independently corroborated implementation examples before identifying products, integrations, or outcomes.

content.title: Credit administration and independent review
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Credit decision"] -->|"Establishes approved terms"| B["Credit administration"]
  B -->|"Maintains supporting information"| C["Ongoing monitoring"]
  C -->|"Identifies deterioration"| D["Remedial management"]
  E["Independent credit review"] -->|"Assesses administration and monitoring"| C
  E -->|"Reports findings"| F["Board and senior management"]
```
content.summary: This conceptual diagram summarizes international credit-management guidance. It does not document an Iranian bank's organizational structure or deployed software.

name: Banking Customer Management
description: Banking customer management connects verified identity, account relationships, and information maintained throughout a customer's relationship with a bank. In Iran, published regulatory material links account-based services to national customer-identification infrastructure, although current implementation requires further verification.

seo.title: Banking Customer Management in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Customer identity, ongoing due diligence, and reliable banking records, with clearly stated gaps in current Iranian implementation evidence.

content.heading: Understanding the customer relationship
content.content:
Customer management in banking involves more than maintaining a name and contact address. The Financial Action Task Force, the intergovernmental body that sets international standards against money laundering and terrorist financing, distinguishes identifying a customer, verifying representatives, identifying beneficial owners, and understanding the intended relationship. A beneficial owner is the individual who ultimately owns or controls the customer. [s1]

These distinctions are especially useful for understanding business accounts: the company, its representative, and its ultimate owner need not be the same person. The international framework is an explanatory benchmark here; it does not establish Iranian legal requirements or demonstrate compliance by an Iranian institution. [s1]

content.heading: Iran's published identification framework
content.content:
A reproduced Iranian directive on banking-transaction transparency, identified as adopted on Solar Hijri 1401/12/27, states that account-based banking operations depend on obtaining a Shahab identifier through the Nahab system. In this context, Nahab is the system used to obtain that customer identifier. The reproduced text also says that obtaining Shahab does not remove a bank's other customer-identification responsibilities. [s2]

This is evidence of a published rule's wording, not proof of its present enforcement. The inspected material was a legal reproduction rather than an authenticated Central Bank publication. Subsequent amendments, exceptions, and current operational procedures remain unverified. [s2]

content.heading: Keeping information useful over time
content.content:
International due-diligence standards describe an ongoing process: transactions are considered against knowledge of the customer's business and risk profile, and relevant records are reviewed and updated. Successful onboarding therefore does not make customer information permanently complete. [s1]

Reliable records also require consistent definitions and reconciliation. Basel's risk-data principles recommend an authoritative source for each type of risk data and a shared dictionary of concepts. Applied to customer information, this suggests an evaluation question: can the bank explain how records used in lending and risk reporting refer to the same customer? This is an editorial inference from the guidance, not a verified description of Iranian systems. [s3]

The central distinction is between possessing an identifier and maintaining a well-supported understanding of a relationship. Publication of a fuller Iran-specific account requires authoritative rules and documented implementation evidence.

name: Treasury Systems
description: Bank treasury systems bring together information about cash obligations, funding, and collateral to support liquidity decisions. For Iran, historical evidence explains why funding arrangements matter, but current operating rules and bank-level deployments require further verification.

seo.title: Bank Treasury Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to bank liquidity, funding, collateral, and treasury data, distinguishing general principles from verified Iranian practice.

content.heading: Having funds available when obligations fall due
content.content:
Liquidity concerns a bank's ability to meet cash and collateral obligations without unacceptable losses. The US Federal Reserve describes liquidity-risk management as anticipating funding needs and coordinating available resources under normal and stressed conditions. This definition helps explain the purpose of treasury systems; it is not an Iranian regulatory requirement. [s1]

A treasury view must consider timing as well as amounts. An expected receipt later in the day may not cover a payment due earlier. Similarly, an asset's recorded value does not by itself establish whether cash can be raised from it when needed. These are practical implications of managing cash and collateral obligations across time. [s1]

content.heading: Connecting forecasts, funding, and collateral
content.content:
Basel liquidity guidance emphasizes cash-flow projections, funding concentrations, collateral, stress tests, and contingency funding plans. It also distinguishes intraday needs from longer funding horizons. A useful conceptual treasury system therefore connects expected flows with available resources and the conditions under which those resources can be used. [s2]

This does not mean every forecast is certain. Normal assumptions and stressed assumptions serve different purposes. The diagram below summarizes an analytical relationship, rather than prescribing a transaction sequence or documenting an Iranian implementation. [s2]

content.title: From liquidity information to a funding response
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Expected cash inflows and outflows"] -->|"Inform"| C["Liquidity assessment"]
  B["Available funding and collateral"] -->|"Constrain feasible responses"| C
  D["Stress assumptions"] -->|"Test resilience"| C
  C -->|"Identifies potential shortfalls"| E["Funding response and contingency plan"]
```
content.summary: Cash-flow expectations, usable resources, and stress assumptions inform liquidity assessment. The arrows show analytical inputs and outputs, not legal authority or a guaranteed ability to obtain funding.

content.heading: Iranian context and the limits of software
content.content:
In its 2018 Iran consultation, IMF staff described liquidity-management plans associated with access to central-bank emergency lending and recommended changes to lending facilities. These observations explain the historical importance of funding arrangements, but they should not be read as current facility terms. [s3]

Data reliability is equally important. A Basel Committee newsletter published in January 2026 identifies persistent international challenges involving fragmented systems, data lineage, and timely reporting. Data lineage means being able to trace information from its origin to its final use. The newsletter reports international experience, not an assessment of Iran. [s4]

For this page, the resulting evaluation question is whether a treasury report can explain its inputs, assumptions, and constraints. A dashboard alone cannot demonstrate that funding will remain available in stress. Current Iranian market-operation rules, collateral conditions, and documented bank practices are needed to complete the local account. [s2][s4]
